searchText: IMO, terms are being used in different situations, many times with marketing objectives and not tech ones. As some networks that claim to be sidechains. We should avoid discussing (on the bad meaning) about that, because any terms that becomes popular will star being used by marketmen. As being a decentralized community it's tough to have someone take the authority to set what technologies should or shouldn't use a term. that text fails to explain the difference of L2 and rollup to claim they're different things, and basicaly "there are many different rollup implementations and they're useful for many use cases" doesn't make them not L2 If we consider tx spam as actually flooding tx, as bots flooding the network with tx fighting each other for who commits their tx first, and that all tx are worth if commited, then I'd say the cause is indeed low cost tx and therefore the solution would be increasing tx fee. Other solutions would be limit the minimum duration an account may submit a tx or only increase tx fee for accounts willing to flood. But all these sorts of solutions may be bypassed by the same user using hundreds of different accounts to fake as hundreds of different users. Then we'd need to throw privacy away to be able to identify when the same user is using multiple accounts. If we consider tx spam as a bad actor spamming the network for DDOS or the sorts, then the situation is more complex and only higher tx fee would be able to avoid that, I'm afraid. Thank you so much! This is exactly what i'm asked about i saw at least 3 cases with successful attacks to networks with pretty solid dev teams and it raised my concern regarding L2 reliability to keep low tx cost I feel that most L2 providers are running their instances on centralized systems. Some are charging low fees because it's very cheap and some aren't even charging tx fees and instead charge % over trades. I haven't seen any atk on any L2 yet, I also wonder how they'd react. Maybe they'd reboot the server and lock funds of attackers. running their instances which is absolutely awesome but for private/corporate networks flood attacks mainly cripple networks that try to scale past what they should be able to, block space is a pretty efficient market in networks that have more constrained L1 block space which keeps verification costs relatively low but what about more open https://www.reddit.com/r/maticnetwork/comments/o1hpl7/there_is_an_active_spam_attack_happening_to/ nano network had the same problem and I was wonder what they will do - and as you said - they increased tx fee. Not an ideal solution. That's the problem like there is no good solution that doesn't involve raising tx fees or just accepting the increased costs of verifying the ledger which is even worse because then you compromise on decentralization the way around it is by reducing the number of parties that need to be involved in a transaction in order for it to settle and/or reducing the overall cost of a transaction, which you do with L2s And anyone that says otherwise doesn't actually care about resistance to attack Note that L2s and their (centralized) sequencers can also decide to censor certain transactions to mitigate spam (but exit via L1 remains uncensorable, albeit costly) yeah, looks like solution should consider the project with understanding these dependencies, like: a) resistance to attack => less privacy & decentralization, but low tx fees, or b) doesn't care about resistance => more openness & decentralization, but with risk of tx cost increase this isn't an inherent property of rollups though and there's designs for blind sequencers and other L2 designs such as payment channel networks don't suffer from that issue at all Well, you kind of need a base layer (=L1) to always be able to exit to (bypassing the sequencer), so that's why I'd say it's only possible as an L2. sorry I meant about the sequencers being centralized and having the ability to censor Ah, no, there's plenty of designs that allow for such scenarios indeed Either way I'm interested to see how prevalent spam attacks really would be with fee markets in place. Things get really expensive really fast. (If we're talking about spam attacks as in "filling blocks with useless txs such that no one else fits in anymore") DDoS seems more likely imo, i.e. overloading the networking stack submit over tor lol

excerpts.author: hikariws
excerpts.content: that text fails to explain the difference of L2 and rollup to claim they're different things, and basicaly "there are many different rollup implementations and they're useful for many use cases" doesn't make them not L2

excerpts.author: hikariws
excerpts.content:
If we consider tx spam as actually flooding tx, as bots flooding the network with tx fighting each other for who commits their tx first, and that all tx are worth if commited, then I'd say the cause is indeed low cost tx and therefore the solution would be increasing tx fee.

Other solutions would be limit the minimum duration an account may submit a tx or only increase tx fee for accounts willing to flood. But all these sorts of solutions may be bypassed by the same user using hundreds of different accounts to fake as hundreds of different users. Then we'd need to throw privacy away to be able to identify when the same user is using multiple accounts.

excerpts.author: hikariws
excerpts.content: If we consider tx spam as a bad actor spamming the network for DDOS or the sorts, then the situation is more complex and only higher tx fee would be able to avoid that, I'm afraid.
